answer_json.answer: A leader resting near its highs

lesson_text: A leader resting in a box near its highs. That's a flat base. Look left and you see a strong run. Then the stock goes sideways in a tight range just under the top, above its rising averages. Nobody's dumping it. That's what I want, because the box gives you two things. A clear top to buy through, and a stop that sits close, a few cents under the breakout day's low. A V-bottom or a stock under its 200-day gives you neither. A flat base is a leader resting near its highs. The box gives you the trigger and the stop.

answer_json.answer: The reclaim, as its own setup

lesson_text: The reclaim. Once it undercut the floor, the flat base was over. But it took 71 back in two days. That's a shakeout. The dip flushed out weak holders, and buyers stepped right back in. We call it an undercut and reclaim, a U&R. It's its own trade, with its own trigger and its own stop. How fast a reclaim has to come is a judgment call. Two days is quick. Lose the floor and the box is gone. A fast reclaim is its own trade.

Keep a piece on the trail in case it keeps going. Just don't give the whole move back waiting. When the whole move happens in three days, that's the strength to sell into.

answer_json.answer: A short rest after a near-double

lesson_text: A short rest after a near-double. That's a high tight flag. IOVA more than doubled in about five weeks, then sat a little under its high without handing much back. When a stock rests like that after a run like that, the holders aren't selling. Volume dries up, the closes stay tight, and the gains from the pole stay put. These are rare. When I see one, it goes straight on my radar. A high tight flag is a near-double that rests a few weeks just under the high.

answer_json.answer: A quiet base, then a real change

lesson_text: A quiet base, then a real change. That's a sleeper waking up. It sat quiet for months, then earnings, a product or a contract gave big buyers a reason to show up. A run like that has real buyers behind it. A bounce off a crash only wins back what was lost, so it's a repair, not a new leg. And a third leg late in a huge run is where tired moves end. I want the sleeper. A sleeper that wakes up on real news is the start you want, not a crash bounce.

answer_json.answer: Closes bunch up, wide wicks or not

lesson_text: The closes bunch up. Where a stock closes is where buyers and sellers settled for the day. So when the closes hold one tight area, the holders are staying put, even if the wicks swing around intraday. That's what tight means to me. On AMD here, judge the closes, not the wicks. A rest that closes all over the place is loose, and I pass on those. Judge a flag by where it closes, not by its wicks.

lesson_text: A Wedge Drop. The stock stalled near its rising averages for about two weeks, then closed down through both. That's the pop's mirror. A pop rests under the averages and breaks up through them. A drop rests up at them and breaks down. For a long, that's a sell signal, not a buy. If you're holding the rest on a trail, that close under both averages takes you out. Same coil, opposite door. Where it closes tells you which.

lesson_text: A dead stock re-priced by big news. That's the whole setup in one line. The stock's been flat or down for months and nobody cares about it. Then a real surprise hits. Because it never rallied into the news, none of that news is in the price yet. So the gap is the market re-pricing it in one morning, and that's why the move can run for weeks. Before I call anything an EP, I look at the six months before the gap. Neglect plus a real surprise. That's the whole idea.

lesson_text: Buy it, with the stop a few cents under the inside day's low. The gap held for two days, so the delayed entry is live. Then day three went quiet, an inside day. That tight little range gives you a tight trigger. Its high is 59.91 and its low is 2.3% below, inside the 1 to 3% we like. WING did exactly this and ran to 11.4R at its best. If the break fails, you lose a little. An inside day after the gap gives you a tight trigger and a tight stop.

There's no fresh story here, and no flood of new owners, because everyone already owns it. It's not a PEG either. A Power Earnings Gap, PEG for short, is an earnings gap on big but ordinary volume. No report, no PEG. A big day in a mega-cap isn't an edge.

choices: Just a big day, not an HVE
An HVE, it's a one-year record
An HVE, it closed up on volume
prompt_json.q: Is it an HVE, a Power Earnings Gap, or just a big day?
prompt_json.story: A mega-cap everyone owns trades its biggest volume in a year. That's about 3 times its average, and it closes up 7%. No earnings report.
prompt_json.subject: SET.21#q56

deeper.trap: Rank the volume against the stock's own history and its size. Greg Duncan puts it well: the focus isn't any high volume but the highest volume. A mega-cap's big day is ordinary for a name that size, so it fails the lesser-known test before the news even lands.

sources.name: Our High Volume Edge playbook
sources.quote: Calling any year-high volume an HVE: a 3x day on a mega-cap is an HVC. … hve.lesser_known: a mega-cap or a well-owned large cap (AAPL, ASML, ORCL were cut) … Rank the volume, not the gap. An earnings gap on big but ordinary volume in a well-owned name is a PEG … A lesser-known stock: 50-day dollar volume under about $100 million a day before the event. Not a mega-cap. … A fresh story: a contract, a trial result, a partnership, a government stake, an IPO-year re-rating, or earnings so big the volume is extreme. Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.

sources.name: Greg Duncan: Trading The High Volume Close Setup (Upside Unlimited, 2023-12-02)
sources.quote: Our focus in the HVC setup is not just on any high volume but on the highest volume.

The PEG tell: big but ordinary volume in a well-owned name is a PEG. Lesser-known: under about $100 million a day before the event; not a mega-cap. A fresh story; earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.

answer_json.answer: Stopped out, a small planned loss

lesson_text: Stopped out for a small planned loss. 47.52 is 1.7% under your 48.34 buy. Day 3 opened at 49.56, reversed to 46.94 and ran right through it. The stop order sold you out while you were at work. That's its whole job. A stop in your head would've sat there while you weren't looking. Tight day-2 stops keep the loss small when the trade fails. A real stop order acts when you can't. That's its job.

That gives a normal shake a little more room. The outer limit is the bottom of the pullback, never past it. More room means fewer shares, because the size comes from the distance to the stop. The low of the day is still our first choice. Wider means the lower of two days' lows. The pullback's bottom is the limit.

answer_json.answer: The turn after a 3 to 5 day crash

lesson_text: It's the turn after a 3 to 5 day crash. Take Bracco's parabolic burst and flip it upside down. A stock falls straight down for days, gaps down one last time, then snaps back. We buy the snap back, never the fall. Think of a rubber band: stretch it that far that fast and it wants to pull back toward its averages. That pull is the edge. It's also why we wait for the turn instead of guessing the bottom. We buy the snap back, not the fall.

lesson_text: Hold. The pivot is a swing entry with a tight stop. We very rarely sell on day 1, and the first sell waits until day 3 at the earliest. Selling it all at 1R to 2R treats it like a day trade, and that's where the big winners get cut off. The tight stop makes 3R and 5R come fast. DELL hit 3R the same afternoon and 5R the next morning. A pivot is a swing entry with a tight stop. Let it become a swing.

reveal_json.lesson_line: Most of these get stopped. Ride the ones that work.
reveal_json.simple: Trail the winners. Most buys get stopped, so the few runners have to be ridden.
reveal_json.why: Trail the winners. In our test most buys got stopped, 88.2% of them inside 60 days. The few that ran have to pay for all of those. wrong.Buy only the tiniest bars: Tinier isn't better. A sliver's low sits right in the day's noise.
wrong.Size up on every buy: Bigger size makes every loss bigger too. Size comes from the stop, not from hope.
wrong.Use a wider stop: A wider stop just means fewer shares for the same risk. It does nothing for the winners.

lesson_text: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. The reason is getting out. Own a big chunk of a day's trading and when you sell, you're the one pushing the price down on yourself. It's a ceiling, not a target. Your risk math sets the size, and this just caps it. One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

answer_json.answer: A bounce after a short, fast drop

lesson_text: A bounce after a short, fast drop. When a strong stock gets hit way harder and faster than normal, it ends up stretched far under its short averages. Stretched things snap back. We're trading that snapback, a swing of a few days back toward those averages. It's not a breakout and it's not a long hold. And it's not any stock that's down a lot. It's a leader that got flushed, because a trend has to exist before mean reversion can kick in. We trade the snapback after a leader gets flushed, not the drop itself.

lesson_text: No. Two red days and a 3% gap on average volume is a normal dip for a leader. Nothing's stretched yet. Breaking the 50-day doesn't make it a flush either. A drive day that closes in the bottom third of its range, or under its open, is a drive that failed. 24% is in the bottom third, so I don't like it. But we don't add an exit we never planned. Just don't add to it, and don't widen anything. A weak close is a warning, not an order. The stop is the exit.

reveal_json.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell. Write it before the bell, then just execute.
reveal_json.simple: Buy at market through 277.23, stop just under 272.80, and make the first sell on day 3 or later.
reveal_json.why: Market 277.24, stop 272.75, first sell day 3 or later. The trigger is the first trade through 277.23, so your market order fills around 277.24. The low of the day is the first bar's low, 272.80, and the stop goes a few cents under it at 272.75. That's 1.6% away, nice and tight. Then the first sell is a judgment, and I very rarely make it on day one. LRCX hit 3R at the next morning's open and ran to 16.8R at its best. Sell on day one and you've thrown away the part that pays.

wrong.Limit 275.00, stop 268.00, sell at 2R: A limit under the trigger won't fill on the break, and 268.00 is nowhere near the low of the day.
wrong.Market 277.24, stop 272.75, sell day one: Right entry, right stop. But we very rarely sell on day one, and this one ran to 16.8R.

lesson_text: 203.32. 208.00 minus 205.66 is 2.34, and that's 1R. Two of them is 4.68. Take that off your fill and you're at 203.32. Here's why you want that number before the open. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes your new stop. If those first 30 minutes take you past 2R, under 203.32, you're out. Know the line ahead of time and there's nothing to decide in the panic. Know your 2R price before the gap. The first 30 minutes decide.

lesson_text: Switching plans mid-trade. You pick the plan before you buy, and you keep it. The switch is where it goes wrong. You planned a hold, it dips, and you scalp it for a small loss. Or you planned a scalp, it runs, and you hold it all the way back down. Either way you're deciding with money on the line instead of with a clear head. We work the same way: entry, stop and size get written down before the market opens. Pick the plan before you buy. Changing it mid-trade is the mistake.

Picking a scalp on the open

lesson_text: 8,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 850,000 times 0.01 is 8,500. That's a ceiling, not a target, and your risk math will most often land under it. Here's why it exists. If you own a big chunk of what trades in a day, you can't get out fast when you need to. Your own selling pushes the price against you. It's the same reason we don't even watch illiquid names. Size to the volume. One percent of an average day is the ceiling.

lesson_text: The Parabolic Short. Day 4 of a run with stacked gap ups is a parabolic burst. A euphoric gap that drives and then fails is the climax. Bracco calls that failed drive the U-Turn. It belongs to the Parabolic Short, the one short we allow above the 200-day, and only because it's parabolic. It's not a drive to hold, and it's not a Kicker, since there's no red day before the gap. Shorting is only for traders who've already made $1 million trading. On day 3 to 5 of a burst, a failed up-drive is the U-Turn, a climax short.

choices: A Kicker, it gapped up again
An Episodic Pivot, a news gap
